title: SpaceX caught Starship from orbit with ‘robot chopsticks’ in a world 1st — but lost its booster in the Gulf of Mexico
detail:
SpaceX caught Starship from orbit with ‘robot chopsticks’ in a world 1st — but lost its booster in the Gulf of Mexico
Rudro Chakrabarti

SPCX
GOOG
TSLA

"This is actually a bigger deal for humanity than most people can imagine," Walter Isaacson, Elon Musk's biographer, wrote on X after SpaceX (NASDAQ: SPCX) caught its Starship spacecraft with the launch tower's arms on Nov. 14. Musk shared the post with a message of his own: "The epic day has arrived, thanks to the incredibly talented team at SpaceX!"

Isaacson also recalled the engineers' reactions in a Starbase conference room in December 2020, when Musk pushed the idea that the tower's arms could catch a returning Starship.

After about 22.5 hours and 14 orbits, Starship returned to SpaceX's Starbase site in Texas, and the tower's mechanical arms plucked it out of the air. "Mechazilla catches Starship!" SpaceX posted. It was the first catch of a spacecraft returning from orbit.

Hours after the catch, Musk reshared his Aug. 30, 2021, post calling the tower arms "robot chopsticks," which warned that "success is not guaranteed, but excitement is!" On Flight 15, he got half of each. The rocket's Super Heavy booster, which was supposed to be caught the same way, was diverted and exploded in the Gulf of Mexico. SpaceX has caught three earlier versions of the booster, the first in October 2024, but this was the first attempt with its newest design.

SpaceX shares closed at $139.11 on Nov. 13, about 3% above the $135 IPO price, then slipped about 2% in after-hours trading as the booster was lost. Nov. 16 is the market's first chance to react to the catch. The next test comes Dec. 8, when the last batch of insider shares from the IPO lockup can be sold.

What actually happened in Texas

Starship Flight 15 lifted off at 5:47 p.m. ET on Nov. 13 from Starbase, with the booster's 33 Raptor engines producing more than 18 million pounds of thrust. It was SpaceX's first attempt to catch both stages of the rocket, with the booster due back minutes after launch and the ship, known as Ship 42, the following afternoon.

The booster's guidance system decided it wasn't lined up for a tower catch and sent it toward the Gulf instead.

Ship 42 kept climbing into orbit, which Starship first reached on the previous flight, on Sept. 28. About 35 minutes after liftoff, it began releasing 26 Starlink V3 satellites, a batch SpaceX says adds roughly 10 times the downlink capacity of a Falcon 9 Starlink launch. Three of the satellites carried cameras to photograph the ship's heat shield, which SpaceX checked before committing to bring it home. The ship then circled Earth about 14 times.

On Dec. 9, Rivian Automotive (NASDAQ:RIVN) hosts its second annual Autonomy and AI Day. Taking a page from the Tesla playbook, Rivian hosts this event to showcase its latest autonomous-vehicle innovations to investors.

Last year's event elicited mixed reactions, but Wall Street could sing a different tune this year if it perceives that Rivian's Autonomy Plus, its subscription-based driver-assistance platform, will help the electric car company continue to scale up and add to its recent R2-related success.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Rivian Automotive.

Rivian Autonomy and AI Day preview

Expect Point-to-Point, Rivian's hands-free, door-to-door driver-assistance capability, to be front and center at next month's Autonomy and AI Day. Recently, Rivian announced plans for an invitation-only early access program that will enable select Autonomy Plus subscribers to test the new feature before a full launch in 2027.

The market knows about Point-to-Point, but one analyst, Stifel's Stephen Gengaro, believes that the event, plus the increasing importance of autonomous driving features as a product differentiator, could make further details of its launch an important catalyst for the stock. Gengaro gives shares a "buy" rating and a $22-per-share price target, which is around two-thirds above Rivian's current stock price.

The takeaway for investors

Rivian's autonomous driving events come on the heels of its well-received third-quarter 2026 earnings release. For the quarter, the company reported nearly $2.2 billion in revenue, a 38% year-over-year increase, driven largely by the success of its R2 midsize SUV. Rivian's top line exceeded Wall Street expectations, as did its reported gross profit of $176 million. Analysts expected $39 million in gross profit on $2 billion in sales.

Rivian also beat expectations on Q4 delivery guidance. Although shares rallied immediately after earnings, this rally has since lost momentum. Investors' focus may be shifting back to other concerns, such as Rivian's timeline to reach full profitability. While such concerns could persist after Dec. 9, this event could still shift focus back to the growth story, triggering another rally for what remains one of the most popular electric car stocks.

A billionaire who went big on Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) this year just closed his wallet.

"No further investment without Jensen," billionaire Leo KoGuan told Bloomberg (1) in a text message, a day after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO. KoGuan, best known as one of the largest individual shareholders in Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) and worth about $13.2 billion by Bloomberg's estimate, said he has put about $1.3 billion into the chipmaker, though Bloomberg couldn't independently verify that figure. His pledge covers new purchases; he didn't say he'd sell the shares he already owns.

Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, resigned as president, CEO and board member effective immediately, Nvidia announced Nov. 12. The board accepted his resignation Nov. 11, according to a regulatory filing. CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO, and the board said Nov. 13 it was still choosing a search firm to find a permanent replacement. Huang himself has been involved in that search and has personally contacted at least one potential candidate, The Washington Post reported (2), citing people familiar with the matter. His exit followed reports of extramarital relationships, including one with a former Megaspeed executive who U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspect (3) was recruited by China's top spy agency. Beijing has denied she is a spy.

Two heavyweight fund managers, whose names also appear on the petition, have asked the board to pump the brakes in a formal letter.

Here's why the money crowd is so rattled — and why the risk for shareholders may not end with who runs the company.

'The supreme creator': The big money in Huang's corner

KoGuan hasn't been subtle. On X (5), he called Huang "the supreme creator" and said he hopes to invest in any new company Huang starts or buys.

That's a change of pace for an investor who was loading up earlier this year. In March, KoGuan said he'd doubled his Nvidia stake (6) to 2 million shares.

title: Tesla Is Down 13% in 2026 While the S&P 500 Is Up. Here’s the 1 Catalyst Left This Year That Could Flip That.
detail:
Tesla Is Down 13% in 2026 While the S&P 500 Is Up. Here’s the 1 Catalyst Left This Year That Could Flip That.
Lee Samaha, The Motley Fool

^GSPC
NVDA

Trading disclosure

Tesla's (NASDAQ:TSLA) stock decline this year is partially due to the same reason it could yet turn positive. Specifically, it's the sluggish robotaxi rollout, including the dedicated robotaxi, Cybercab. Simply put, management's previous statements on the timing and scale of the rollout proved overly optimistic for 2026. However, there is a pathway to recovery.

Tesla's robotaxi rollout

The robotaxi metrics that investors were encouraged to follow, namely robotaxi fleet size and city deployments, have failed to impress. Or rather, they failed to impress relative to expectations.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Tesla.

To be fair, management has made some effort to try and reset these expectations, not least by emphasizing a commitment to safety and the importance of refining its next major upgrade of full self-driving (FSD) software, v15, before scaling the robotaxi fleet, and the need to learn and improve operational matters relating to running a robotaxi fleet.

It's easy and tempting to think that Tesla can just tweak some software and push a few buttons in a factory to produce more Cybercabs and send them out into service, but the reality is very different. As such, investors should focus on what really matters: the iterative process of building a microcosm of a robotaxi service that can be scaled later.

Scaling robotaxi isn't easy

The importance and complexity of this can't be overstated. After all, if you scale a robotaxi service with significant imperfections, say safety issues, then the absolute number of high-profile safety incidents will increase in line with the scaling. These increased safety incidents would inevitably create political and regulatory issues, and more such incidents would increase unit costs.

Moreover, if the scaling involves geographic expansion, it could introduce new edge cases and disproportionately magnify safety issues. At the same time, Tesla obviously wants to expand into new geographies to train its neural networks so they can operate without geofencing in the future -- a major advantage of Tesla's approach compared to Waymo's need for geofencing.

Tesla has a massive data advantage over Waymo and others in gathering data from consumer vehicles, but it also needs miles under unsupervised robotaxi operation, notably Cybercab.

Reports suggest Tesla (TSLA) and SpaceX (SPCX) are advancing merger talks, and a deal could be announced as early as next month. As I noted in a previous article, the merger was always a matter of when, not if, and any doubts were laid to rest during SpaceX's Q3 2026 earnings call last month. Elon Musk, who heads both companies, termed the merger a "good idea" during the call and said, "there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the Super Intelligence singularity."

Tesla-SpaceX Merger Might be Announced Soon

The world's richest person also confirmed that the two boards had formed special committees consisting of independent directors to discuss the merger. He also added that being a "conflicted party," he won't be in discussions with the committees. Notably, Tesla stock, which slumped following its Q3 2026 earnings last month, has since rallied, largely because of the anticipated merger.

Meanwhile, SpaceX has a market cap of around $1.9 trillion, while Tesla is valued just under $1.6 trillion. The combined entity would be valued at around $3.5 trillion. Given the recent slump in Nvidia (NVDA) and Microsoft's (MSFT) 'SaaSpocalypse' woes, the combined entity would have a real shot at becoming the world's second-most valuable company, trailing Apple (AAPL). Any post-merger bullishness with a bit of "Musk" magic could make it the world's biggest company.

Musk has long fancied Tesla becoming the world's most valuable company, touting products like robotaxis and Optimus humanoid. During the Q3 2022 earnings call in October 2022, he argued that the company's market cap could one day surpass the combined market cap of Apple and Saudi Aramco. Back then, the combined market cap of these two giants was in the ballpark of $4 trillion, which has since risen to almost $7 trillion. Incidentally, the multi-billionaire has an even more ambitious prediction for SpaceX and sees it growing bigger than the global GDP.

A Tesla-SpaceX Union Might Create the World's Biggest Company

While expecting Tesla to reach the combined market cap of these two giants would have been a tall ask, a Tesla-SpaceX combination might do the trick. Since both companies don't have the earnings to back up their market caps, the possibility of the combined entity achieving that feat would depend on how the artificial intelligence (AI) trade plays out.

title: ‘Tesla of China’ could make cars in Britain as Burnham considers tariffs

‘Tesla of China’ could make cars in Britain as Burnham considers tariffs
Matthew Field
Sun, November 15, 2026 at 2:00 AM EST 4 min read
9868.HK
TSLA
Trade Tesla on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Brian Gu, of Xpeng, next to the company's prototype flying car - AFP via Getty Images/Jade Gao

A company nicknamed the "Tesla of China" is considering manufacturing its vehicles in Britain as Andy Burnham mulls tariffs on Beijing's electric car companies.

Brian Gu, the vice-chairman and president of Xpeng, told The Telegraph it would be "natural to think about local manufacturing" if sales in Britain hit a certain level.

The comments came as the Guangzhou-headquartered company this week announced plans to launch five new luxury vehicles aimed at British buyers.

Xpeng has been seen as a potential challenger to Tesla, pursuing a similar strategy of hi-tech vehicles packed with self-driving technology, while it has also developed humanoid robots.

Its sleek coupes, such as the LO3, share similarities with Tesla's vehicles, pitting the Chinese companies directly against Elon Musk's car business.

At a launch at the luxury Fairmont Windsor Park Hotel on Thursday, Xpeng unveiled the UK version of its LO3 SUV coupe, which it said would start at £32,990 and feature a range of more than 300 miles.

The Xpeng LO3, pictured at a trade fair in Germany, is pitted directly against Tesla

Speaking to The Telegraph, Mr Gu said the company would consider building vehicles in Britain if its launch in the market is a success.

Mr Gu said: "It depends on the success that we anticipate from these launches. We hope to generate a substantial business. And once we reach a certain volume, then it's natural to think about local manufacturing."

It comes as the Prime Minister considers imposing tariffs on Chinese electric cars. The EU has already enforced steep tariffs of up to 35.3pc on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) and the Prime Minister has been seeking closer ties with Europe, raising the prospect the UK will adopt similar rules.

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, has been drafting a tariff blueprint and Anas Sarwar, the trade minister, said last month that Britain and the EU must "work together and act in lockstep" to combat the flood of Chinese EV imports.

Xpeng's latest UK vehicles will be built in China and shipped to Britain, meaning they would fall foul of any prospective tariff regime. It also produces cars for Europe out of a factory in Austria, although this plant is already near full capacity.

He Xiaopeng, the chief executive of Xpeng, launched the GX car at the Beijing Auto Show in April - AFP via Getty Images/Danai Howard

Xpeng's launch in Britain follows a flood of other Chinese car brands that have swept across the UK market. The Jaecoo 7, made by China's Chery, was the UK's top-selling car in September, while BYD, which makes electric cars such as the Seal, has claimed close to 10pc of EV and hybrid sales so far this year.

The European tariffs have prompted Chinese carmakers to shift more production into the bloc to avoid the levies.

detail:

Prosper Junior Bakiny, The Motley Fool

SPCX
NVDA

Elon Musk-led publicly traded corporations, Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) and Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX), remain volatile. In the days following the U.S. midterm election, they shed a combined $420 billion in market value. Both companies recovered most of these losses and are now back around their pre-election levels, but this recent episode highlighted the extent to which Tesla and SpaceX are exposed to political risk. It's worth digging deeper into it and discussing the potential implications for investors considering either stock.

Image source: Getty Images.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Will the government crack down on Tesla and SpaceX?

Tesla and SpaceX's prospects largely hinge on their artificial intelligence (AI)-related investments. Consider first the case of Tesla. The company's Optimus robot and especially its robotaxi ambitions are the reason the stock continues to command high earnings multiples, despite a mixed (at best) performance from its core electric vehicle (EV) business over the past two years.

Tesla needs considerable computing capacity to train AI models behind its Full Self-Driving (FSD) software and its Optimus humanoid robot. That's why the recent election results could create a problem for the company, as voters elected officials who ran on limiting data center expansion.

But that's just one of the many issues it could face. Several other aspects of Tesla's business could come under regulatory scrutiny, potentially triggering congressional probes. Tesla's recent launch of the Cybercab, which attracted scrutiny from regulators as soon as it hit the road, could once again come under investigation. If it does, it would be a blow to one of Tesla's most promising business ventures, potentially forcing the market to adjust its expectations accordingly.

Musk's other business, SpaceX, is perhaps even more exposed to regulatory risk and to the threat posed by the recent election to the AI industry.

SpaceX is looking to significantly increase computing capacity next year to meet strong demand for its AI services. These plans might not go as the company expects if regulators and lawmakers crack down on data center expansion. Further, some lawmakers recently looked into investigating whether SpaceX restricted Ukrainian military access to its Starlink and Starshield satellite services and whether the U.S. military has become too dependent on the company.
